name: Selenium disulfide
lead: Selenium disulfide (selenium sulfide) is a topical antifungal and keratolytic agent used in shampoos for dandruff, scalp seborrheic dermatitis and tinea versicolor. People use it to clear visible flaking and scalp irritation so that hair and shoulders look clean, and, for tinea versicolor, to treat discoloured patches on the skin of the trunk and neck. As used in products it is better described as a mixture of eight-membered selenium sulfide ring compounds than a single pure compound.[1][2]

It entered US medical use in 1951 and is on the WHO Essential Medicines List.[2] The best-known OTC product is Selsun Blue (1% selenium disulfide).[2] A 2015 clinical-evidence review described it as an alternative once other treatments such as ketoconazole have been tried, while more recent shampoo studies have compared it directly with ketoconazole and zinc pyrithione.[2][12][13]

In looksmaxxing and grooming discussion it comes up as one of several medicated-shampoo actives, alongside ketoconazole, zinc pyrithione and coal tar, for people dealing with dandruff, oily scalp or seborrheic dermatitis. It is a scalp-condition treatment and has not been studied as a hair-growth product.

paras: The main appearance-related use is controlling dandruff and scalp seborrheic dermatitis, whose flakes, redness and itching are visible on hair, scalp and clothing. Wikipedia says symptoms frequently return when treatment stops, so shampoos are often used repeatedly or on a maintenance schedule.[2] Tinea versicolor, a Malassezia-related skin condition, is the other labelled use, and the shampoo or lotion is applied to affected areas of the body.[2][6]

Uses are dandruff, scalp seborrheic dermatitis and tinea versicolor.[2] Wikipedia reports that a 2015 review found limited evidence based on one trial, and that research on hyperkeratosis, scalp psoriasis and dry-eye conditions rests on small series or trials in progress.[2] A small case series of three patients suggested benefit in hyperkeratosis, and clinical observation of more than 100 patients was reported for scalp psoriasis.[2]

The single randomised trial identified by the 2015 review (Danby and colleagues, 1993) enrolled 246 people with moderate-to-severe dandruff for 29 days. Dandruff scores fell by 73% with 2% ketoconazole shampoo (n=97), 67% with 2.5% selenium disulfide (n=100) and 45% with placebo (n=49).[2] The review rated the evidence as low quality and described selenium disulfide as an alternative after other therapies.[2]

More recent work includes a 2023 randomised trial of once-weekly 1% selenium disulfide shampoo versus vehicle for eight weeks, as maintenance after a two-week corticosteroid/salicylic acid course in moderate-to-severe scalp seborrheic dermatitis,[10] a multicentre observational study of a selenium disulfide shampoo applied for four weeks,[11] and a 2023 retrospective chart review of 400 patients (200 on zinc pyrithione and 200 on selenium disulfide) that found no significant difference in relapse timing between the two maintenance shampoos.[12] A 2026 randomised, double-blind trial of 87 people with moderate-to-severe dandruff compared 0.6% micronized selenium disulfide shampoo with 2% ketoconazole over six weeks, with the authors reporting comparable efficacy and cosmetic advantages.[13] An older 1983 trial compared miconazole nitrate and selenium disulfide as anti-dandruff agents.[14] A 2025 editorial reviews what randomised trials show about efficacy and safety in seborrheic dermatitis.[15]

Reported effects with scalp use are infrequent: in the 100-person arm of the early trial, itching or burning (3 people), eruption near the hairline (1), hair lightening (2), orange scalp staining (1) and a chemical taste during shampooing (1) were recorded. It can discolour nails, light hair, dyes and metal jewellery; case reports describe orange to red-brown scalp discolouration that resolved after stopping.[2]

Temporary diffuse hair loss appears in case reports (including a 1956 report in JAMA), and excessive environmental or occupational selenium exposure has been linked to hair loss, but hair loss was not reported with topical selenium disulfide in several large studies.[2] It should not be applied to damaged skin, where absorption is higher; systemic selenium toxicity can cause tremor, weakness, lethargy and abdominal symptoms that usually resolve within about ten days. Use in young children is not recommended, and pregnancy and breastfeeding have not been studied.[2]

It acts as an antifungal against Malassezia yeasts associated with dandruff and as a keratolytic that loosens scale; the detailed molecular mechanism is not well described.[2] A 2023 review proposes that it helps rebalance the scalp microbiome and sebum quality.[4]

In humans, shampoo or lotion use does not normally raise circulating or urinary selenium. It is much less toxic than other selenium salts, which Wikipedia attributes to its low aqueous solubility and very poor systemic absorption; systemic absorption can occur through damaged skin.[2]

Selenium disulfide has an approximate formula of SeS2 but is a mixture of eight-membered ring compounds with an overall selenium-to-sulfur ratio of 1:2. It has negligible solubility in water and a melting point of about 111 C. Past medicinal preparations used elemental selenium, selenium monosulfide and sulfur, which created some confusion about which form a product contained.[2] A 2024 materials-chemistry article discusses producing selenium disulfide from sustainable sources.[16]

In the US, 1% is sold over the counter and 2.5% by prescription. In Canada a 2.5% strength is available OTC. In the UK it is pharmacy-only, in Australia it is a Schedule 5 medicine, and in the EU only 1% is available, with Belgium, the Netherlands and Poland reported to have banned it.[2] Brand names include Selsun Blue and Selseb.[2] Because the active ingredients are generic and cannot be patented, Wikipedia says companies have turned toward new delivery systems and targets.[2]

A 2022 study examined scalp microbiome changes and clinical improvement in mild-to-moderate seborrheic dermatitis using a selenium disulfide shampoo after initial ketoconazole treatment.[3] A 2023 review in the European Journal of Dermatology discusses it for rebalancing scalp microbiome and sebum quality in dandruff.[4] Registered studies include a trial of a 1% selenium disulfide and 1% salicylic acid shampoo on scalp lipids and water loss (NCT05503706),[5] a 2019 study of the same combination on scalp microbiota after ketoconazole in 80 people (NCT04057950),[17] a 60-person efficacy study in dandruff (NCT05506592),[18] a 2005 trial of selenium sulfide, ketoconazole and ciclopirox shampoos as additional treatment for tinea capitis in 47 people (NCT00127868),[19] and a randomised trial of 1.8% selenium sulfide versus 2% ketoconazole shampoo in pityriasis versicolor (NCT04007237).[6]

timeline.event: Introduced for medical use in the United States.[2]
JAMA case report describes temporary hair loss with selenium sulfide shampoo.[2]
Danby and colleagues report a randomised dandruff trial of ketoconazole, selenium disulfide and placebo.[2]
BMJ Clinical Evidence review finds a single randomised trial for scalp seborrheic dermatitis.[2]

card.summary: An old-school dandruff shampoo active (Selsun Blue); a scalp-condition treatment, not a hair-growth one.
card.note: Can stain light hair and jewellery; avoid damaged skin per labels.

quick.overview:
Selenium disulfide is an antifungal and keratolytic ingredient in dandruff shampoos such as Selsun Blue. It is used for dandruff, scalp seborrheic dermatitis and tinea versicolor.

It is generally regarded as a second option after ketoconazole for seborrheic dermatitis.
quick.mechanism: It acts as an antifungal against Malassezia and loosens scale as a keratolytic; the detailed molecular mechanism is not well described.
quick.risks: Scalp itching, burning, hair lightening, orange staining and discolouration of jewellery are reported. Absorption is higher through damaged skin. Strength limits differ by country.

chain: Shampoo suppresses Malassezia yeast and loosens scale
Less flaking, itch and redness on the scalp
Cleaner-looking hair and scalp; even skin tone where tinea versicolor was present
angle.text: Dandruff flakes and scalp redness are visible, so reducing them changes how hair looks day to day. Selenium disulfide shampoo is used for this and for tinea versicolor patches on the skin.
